statement: A patient with suspected blunt trauma to the thoracolumbar spine must be moved onto the CT scanning gantry. If a pelvic fracture has not yet been radiographically excluded, what is the appropriate technique for moving the patient?
options: Flexion of the hips and knees to reduce pelvic floor tension during the move
Manual lift using a six-person lift-and-slide technique
Application of skeletal traction before any rotational movement is attempted
Standard 90-degree log roll with four team members
A 20-degree roll with inline spinal stabilization
correctOption: A 20-degree roll with inline spinal stabilization
optionExplanations: Flexion of the hips is strictly avoided in suspected spinal trauma as it may exacerbate unstable vertebral fractures.
Modern trauma protocols advocate for the use of scoop stretchers and minimal-degree rolls rather than high-risk manual lifts.
Skeletal traction is a definitive treatment modality for realignment and is not an initial movement technique in the primary survey.
A 90-degree log roll is contraindicated in suspected pelvic fractures as it can disrupt established blood clots and increase intrapelvic volume.
A 20-degree roll is the maximum allowed rotation for patients with suspected pelvic fractures to prevent hemodynamic compromise while still allowing minimal access for positioning.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 357 (Book Page): If patients need to be moved during their primary survey, such as when moving onto the CT scanning gantry, a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilisation should be used.

category: Identify musculoskeletal complications due to achondroplasia
statement: Achondroplasia is classified as an autosomal dominant condition. What is the precise chromosomal location of the gene mutation responsible for this skeletal dysplasia?
options: Long arm of Chromosome 11
Long arm of Chromosome X
Short arm of Chromosome 8
Short arm of Chromosome 4
Long arm of Chromosome 17
correctOption: Short arm of Chromosome 4
optionExplanations: Chromosome 11 is where the EXT2 gene for multiple exostoses is located.
Achondroplasia is autosomal, not X-linked, meaning it affects males and females with equal probability.
Chromosome 8 is where the EXT1 gene for multiple exostoses is located.
The FGFR3 gene, which regulates bone growth, is located on chromosome 4p (the short arm). Mutations here are nearly always G380R substitutions.
Chromosome 17 is associated with Neurofibromatosis Type 1, not achondroplasia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 591 (Book Page): Achondroplasia is caused by a gain-in-function mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, located on the short arm of chromosome (Chr) 4...

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: Radiological identification of occult scaphoid fractures
statement: A patient presents with pain 10 days after a fall on an outstretched hand. Initial radiographs at the time of injury were normal, but clinical tenderness persists in the anatomical snuffbox. Which radiological strategy should be implemented next?
options: Repeat scaphoid-view radiographs after 10–14 days
Immediate ultrasound to look for ligamentous rupture
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Bone mineral density scan to assess for osteoporosis
Routine anteroposterior radiograph of the whole forearm
correctOption: Repeat scaphoid-view radiographs after 10–14 days
optionExplanations: Occult scaphoid fractures often only become visible on radiographs 10-14 days after injury when bone resorption at the fracture line occurs.
Ultrasound is primarily for soft tissues and is not the standard protocol for suspected occult scaphoid bony injury.
Surgery is never indicated without radiographic evidence of a displaced or unstable fracture confirmed by imaging.
DEXA scans measure bone density but do not assist in the diagnosis of an acute traumatic fracture.
Forearm radiographs do not provide the magnification or specialized angles needed to evaluate the carpal bones correctly.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): [The rule of 2s... 2 occasions – sometimes the fracture may not be initially visible; a second series of radiographs should be undertaken after 10–14 days if suspicion of bony injury persists. The classic injury here is a scaphoid fracture.]

category: Define osteoporotic fractures and their clinical features
statement: In elderly patients suffering from osteoporotic fractures of the thoracic spine, which specific clinical presentation is most commonly observed?
options: Complete spinal cord transection with paraplegia
Burst fractures with retropulsion into the canal
Distraction injuries associated with lap-belt usage
Wedge compression fractures from low-energy mechanisms
Rotationally unstable Type C injuries with rib dislocations
correctOption: Wedge compression fractures from low-energy mechanisms
optionExplanations: Osteoporotic wedge fractures are usually stable and rarely result in complete cord transection compared to high-energy traumatic dislocations.
Burst fractures involve axial loading and canal compromise; while they occur, wedge compression is specifically cited as the most common in this population.
Chance fractures (distraction) are associated with high-energy deceleration and lap-belts, not the typical low-energy fall of an osteoporotic patient.
The text identifies wedge compression fractures as the primary injury type for older adults with osteoporotic bone.
Type C injuries involve significant energy transfer and rotation, which are less common in the low-energy context of fragility fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group.

category: Discuss treatment options for scoliosis
statement: According to the standardized classification of idiopathic scoliosis based on the age of onset, a patient who first develops a spinal curvature at the age of 14 years would be categorized as having which type?
options: Adult scoliosis
Juvenile scoliosis
Early-onset scoliosis
Adolescent scoliosis
Infantile scoliosis
correctOption: Adolescent scoliosis
optionExplanations: Adult scoliosis is defined as onset occurring at or after skeletal maturity.
Juvenile scoliosis refers to onset between ages 3 and 10 (within 'Early onset' <10y).
Early-onset scoliosis refers to onset before the age of 10 years.
The table classifies the 11–18 year age group specifically as Adolescent scoliosis.
Infantile scoliosis typically refers to onset before age 3 (or within the 'Early onset' <10y window).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 608 (Book Page): TABLE 44.12 Classification of idiopathic scoliosis. ... Adolescent 11–18 years

category: Identify the clinical presentation and red flag signs indicating severe intra-abdominal injury
statement: A patient arrives with a severe pelvic fracture and hemodynamic instability. Based on established trauma statistics, what is the risk that this patient has a concurrent intra-abdominal bleeding source?
optionExplanations: While 50% of patients have associated extrapelvic bleeding sources in general, the specific risk for intra-abdominal bleeding is lower at 30%.
90% is the risk of having *any* associated injury (e.g., chest, head, limbs), not specifically intra-abdominal bleeding.
10% is an underestimation; the risk of intra-abdominal bleeding in unstable pelvic fractures is significantly higher due to the high energy involved.
Statistically, 30% of patients with unstable pelvic fractures will have a concurrent intra-abdominal source of hemorrhage, requiring laparotomy.
While high-energy trauma often causes multisystem injury, it is not guaranteed (100%) that the source is intra-abdominal.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): [The haemodynamically unstable patient with severe pelvic fracture has a 90% risk of associated injuries and a 30% risk of intra-abdominal bleeding.]

category: Explain the classification of fractures using the AO system
statement: AO metaphyseal fractures are categorized into Types A, B, and C. For a 'Type B' injury involving the proximal tibia, which surgical principle is fundamentally prioritized to optimize long-term joint function?
options: External spanning fixation until secondary consolidation occurs.
Restoration of mechanical axis without addressing the articular step-off.
Intentional induction of hypertrophic non-union.
Relative stability and bridge plating of the metaphysis.
Anatomical reduction of the joint surface and absolute stability.
correctOption: Anatomical reduction of the joint surface and absolute stability.
optionExplanations: Option E is incorrect because external fixation is usually a temporary measure for soft-tissue recovery, not the definitive method for articular restoration.
Option D is incorrect because failure to address articular step-off in Type B or C fractures leads to rapid cartilage wear.
Option B is incorrect as non-union is a complication, never a goal of surgical management.
Option A is incorrect because bridge plating is used for relative stability in diaphyseal or extra-articular patterns, not for articular congruity.
Option C is correct; AO Type B metaphyseal fractures are partial articular, necessitating perfect subchondral restoration to prevent degenerative joint disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): Intra-articular fractures require an anatomical reduction and absolute stability.

category: Identify causes of pathological fractures
statement: Which category of clinical conditions leading to pathological fractures includes osteomalacia and Paget’s disease as primary weakening factors?
options: Metastatic bone disease
Contiguous focus osteomyelitis
Metabolic bone disease
Hematological malignancies
Skeletal dysplasias
correctOption: Metabolic bone disease
optionExplanations: Metastatic bone disease involves secondary deposits from solid tumors like breast or prostate cancer.
Contiguous focus osteomyelitis is an infectious cause where bacteria directly invade bone from an adjacent site.
Metabolic bone diseases like osteomalacia (softening due to Vitamin D deficiency), Paget's (disordered remodeling), and osteoporosis are distinct metabolic causes of pathological fractures.
Hematological malignancies include lymphoma and leukaemia, which are cellular infiltrative processes rather than metabolic deficiencies.
Skeletal dysplasias like achondroplasia are genetic growth disorders, not classified as metabolic bone diseases in this context.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 422 (Book Page): The bone may be weakened by... metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia, Paget’s disease, osteoporosis).

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
statement: A 22-year-old athlete presents with anterolateral groin pain. The clinician suspects femoroacetabular impingement (FAI). Which specific radiographic investigation is considered optimal for the detection of a cam-type lesion in the proximal femur?
options: 45-degree Dunn lateral radiograph.
False profile view of the hip.
Weight-bearing mortise view of the hip.
True Anteroposterior (AP) pelvis radiograph.
Standard 'frog' lateral pelvic radiograph.
correctOption: 45-degree Dunn lateral radiograph.
optionExplanations: The 45-degree Dunn lateral view rotates the femoral head-neck junction into a profile that clearly reveals the abnormal bony 'bump' or cam lesion characteristic of FAI.
The false profile view evaluates anterior coverage of the acetabulum, helpful for diagnosing dysplasia, not specifically cam lesions.
A mortise view is a specific projection for the ankle, not the hip joint.
AP pelvis views are good for overall coverage and lateral center-edge angles but often miss cam lesions on the femoral neck.
The frog lateral view is more commonly used in pediatrics to evaluate for slipped capital femoral epiphysis or Perthes' disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 482 (Book Page): 45° Dunn lateral radiographs of the hip are the optimal projection for detecting the presence of a cam lesion

category: Outline the management plan
statement: In the management plan for a trauma patient suspected of significant haemorrhage, which specific protocol for the administration of Tranexamic Acid (TXA) has been shown to reduce mortality?
options: 500 mg given intravenously every hour for 4 hours starting 5 hours after the injury occurred.
1 gram given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a second 1-gram dose infused over 8 hours.
2 grams given as a single bolus immediately upon arrival at the hospital regardless of time from injury.
A single 1-gram dose given only if the systolic blood pressure is >140 mmHg and the pulse is normal.
1 gram given intramuscularly within the first 6 hours of injury followed by oral therapy.
correctOption: 1 gram given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a second 1-gram dose infused over 8 hours.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Administration after 3 hours is associated with no benefit or increased risk and the dosing intervals are wrong.
Correct. This split-dosing regimen (1g loading bolus then 1g infusion) maintains therapeutic antifibrinolytic levels to stabilize clots and reduce mortality from bleeding.
Incorrect. The two-dose regimen is standard; additionally, TXA must not be given more than 3 hours after injury as it may then be harmful.
Incorrect. TXA is specifically indicated for those with *low* systolic pressure (<110 mmHg) or high pulse (>110 bpm) suggesting significant blood loss.
Incorrect. The route must be intravenous, and the drug should be administered as early as possible, ideally within 1-3 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Tranexamic acid is an antifbrinolytic drug that reduces the risk of mortality from bleeding in both blunt and penetrating trauma. One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours.

category: Describe the common types and mechanisms of extremity trauma
statement: A 7-year-old child presents with a diaphyseal fracture following a fall. Radiographs demonstrate that the bone has failed completely on the convex (tension) side but remains intact on the concave side. What is the fundamental mechanical principle governing this specific injury pattern?
options: Torsional failure resulting in a spiral configuration
Comminution due to high-velocity energy transfer
Failure of the compression cortex with buckling
Elastic recoil following bayonet apposition
Failure of the tension cortex with an intact compression side
correctOption: Failure of the tension cortex with an intact compression side
optionExplanations: Torsional failure leads to spiral fractures where the bone twists; this is a complete failure mode and is not restricted to the tension side of a greenstick injury.
Comminution involves multiple fragments from high-energy transfer; greenstick fractures are by definition simple, incomplete fractures typically from low to moderate energy.
Failure of the compression side with buckling defines a Torus fracture, whereas the question describes failure on the tension (convex) side.

Elastic recoil describes the tendency of bones to return to a baseline position after force removal, which often complicates reduction, but it does not define the mechanical failure of a greenstick pattern.

In a greenstick fracture, the tension (convex) side of the bone fails due to tensile forces while the compression (concave) side remains intact, reflecting the unique plastic properties of pediatric bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): These incomplete fractures are called greenstick (Figure 32.8) fractures, where one tension cortex fails.

category: Interpret characteristic radiographic findings relevant to diagnosis and follow-up
coreConcept: Pathological Radiographic Features of Chronic Osteomyelitis
statement: In the interpretation of a radiograph for suspected chronic osteomyelitis, which specific pathological feature is characterized as a fragment of dead, devascularized bone surrounded by reactive new bone formation?
options: Involucrum
Callus
Brodie’s abscess
Osteophyte
Sequestrum
correctOption: Sequestrum
optionExplanations: The involucrum is the layer of new, living bone that the periosteum lays down around the site of infection to support the weakened bone.
Callus is the reactive bone and cartilage formed during the normal healing of a fracture, specifically in secondary or indirect bone healing.
A Brodie’s abscess is a subacute form of osteomyelitis that presents as a sclerotic-walled cyst on radiographs rather than a free dead fragment.
An osteophyte is a fibrocartilage-capped bony outgrowth typically seen at the margins of joints in degenerative conditions like osteoarthritis.
A sequestrum is a piece of necrotic (dead) bone that has become separated from the surrounding healthy bone during the process of chronic osteomyelitis due to devascularization.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 575 (Book Page): The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments. New bone is laid down around the infection from the periosteum (involucrum).

category: Define septic arthritis and identify its etiological agent
coreConcept: Synovial Fluid Analysis in Septic Arthritis
statement: A patient with suspected septic arthritis of the knee undergoes joint aspiration. Which of the following synovial fuid analysis fndings is most characteristic of acute bacterial infection?
options: Presence of rhomboid-shaped crystals under polarized light
Blood-stained fuid with a protein count of 1 g/dL
White cell count of 5,000 cells/mm3 with 40% neutrophils
Clear fuid with negative Gram stain and glucose level matching serum
White cell count of 80,000 cells/mm3 with >90% neutrophils
correctOption: White cell count of 80,000 cells/mm3 with >90% neutrophils
optionExplanations: Crystals indicate crystal-induced arthropathies like pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate), though they can coexist with infection.
Blood-stained fluid (haemarthrosis) is usually seen in trauma, ligamentous injury, or bleeding disorders.
A count of 5,000 cells/mm3 is more consistent with inflammatory or non-inflammatory conditions like osteoarthritis.
Septic joint fluid is typically purulent and turbid; glucose levels are usually significantly lower than serum levels due to bacterial consumption.
Bacterial septic arthritis typically produces a massive influx of neutrophils, often resulting in counts exceeding 50,000 cells/mm3 and a neutrophil percentage over 90%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 578 (Book Page): A high WCC in joint fuid (e.g. 50–150 000 cells/mm3), with a neutrophil predominance (>90%), is characteristic of infection.

category: Discuss pediatric fractures and their management
statement: A clinician treats a child with a limb deformity by altering mechanical loads to influence bone growth. Which physiological principle states that compressive forces inhibit growth while tensile forces stimulate growth at the physis?
options: Seddon’s classification
Wolff’s law
Hilton’s law
Perren’s theory
Hueter–Volkmann principle
correctOption: Hueter–Volkmann principle
optionExplanations: Seddon’s classification is a clinical system for categorizing the severity of peripheral nerve injuries (neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis).
Wolff’s law states that mature bone deposition and resorption occur in response to stresses applied, governing bone density rather than physeal longitudinal growth.
Hilton’s law states that the nerve supplying a joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin over the insertions of those muscles.
Perren’s theory relates to the amount of interfragmentary strain required for specific types of tissue differentiation during fracture healing (indirect bone healing).
The Hueter-Volkmann principle describes the effect of mechanical pressure on the growth plate itself, which is the basis for using staples or plates in 'guided growth' to correct deformities.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 588 (Book Page): [Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth; Tensile forces stimulate growth.]

category: Describe nutritional roles in recovery from sports injuries
statement: In the context of adolescent athletes suffering from nutritional rickets, what is the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying the bone recovery deficit?
options: Premature fusion of the physis due to axial loading
Excessive production of type I collagen
Inadequate mineralisation of growing bone
Loss of nerve sheath continuity
Failure of segmentation in adjacent tarsal bones
correctOption: Inadequate mineralisation of growing bone
optionExplanations: Premature fusion (epiphysiodesis) can be a complication of trauma, but rickets is characterized by widened, cupped physes.
Type I collagen defects are characteristic of osteogenesis imperfecta, not rickets.
Correct. The fundamental problem in rickets (whether nutritional or genetic) is the failure to properly mineralize the osteoid matrix of growing bone.
Loss of nerve sheath continuity refers to axonotmesis or neurotmesis (Seddon classification), not metabolic bone disease.
Failure of segmentation describes tarsal coalition, which is a structural rather than a metabolic nutritional condition.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 593 (Book Page): In rickets, the primary problem is inadequate mineralisation of growing bone.

category: Explain Salter-Harris classification for growth plate injuries
statement: Which type of Salter-Harris injury is associated with direct trauma to the peripheral structures of the physis, such as the perichondral ring, and was an addition to the original classification by Mercer Rang?
options: Type VI
Type III
Type V
Type II
Type IV
correctOption: Type VI
optionExplanations: Type VI was not in Salter and Harris's original five-part classification. Mercer Rang added it to describe injuries to the perichondral ring (Ranvier’s zone), which is responsible for the appositional (width) growth of the physis. Damage here often leads to peripheral bony bars and severe angulation.
Type III involves the intra-articular epiphyseal surface.
Type V is a generalized axial crush injury.
Type II involves the metaphysis, not specifically the peripheral perichondral ring.
Type IV is a vertical trans-physeal fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): Type VI – injury to perichondral structures by direct trauma. Rare injury, high chance of abnormal growth.

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
statement: Which specific biomechanical characteristic distinguishes an incomplete torus fracture from a complete transverse fracture in the pediatric population?
options: There is a visible fracture line involving both cortical surfaces.
Failure occurs specifically on the tension side of the bone cortex.
The compression cortex buckles due to the plastic nature of immature bone.
The bone undergoes plastic deformation without any visible buckling.
The fracture line involves a total failure across the entire bone diameter.
correctOption: The compression cortex buckles due to the plastic nature of immature bone.
optionExplanations: A visible line through both cortical surfaces indicates a complete fracture, whereas torus fractures lack a traditional through-and-through fracture line.
Failure on the tension side specifically characterizes a greenstick fracture, which is another type of incomplete fracture, not a torus fracture.
A torus (or buckle) fracture is an incomplete injury where the bone fails on the compression side, causing a localized bulge or buckle without a complete break.
Plastic deformation is a type of incomplete injury where the bone bends but lacks a localized buckle or a visible fracture line entirely.
Total failure across the entire bone diameter is the hallmark of a complete fracture, typically seen in adult-type injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 400 (Book Page): In children and adolescents the fracture line may be incomplete because of the plastic, less brittle nature of their bones (Figure 32.7). If the compression cortex buckles, they are called torus (Figure 32.9) or buckle fractures.

category: Define thoracic trauma and classify it into blunt and penetrating types
statement: Which of the following statistics accurately represents the incidence of thoracic injury within the spectrum of severe multisystem trauma?
options: It accounts for 10% of all severe injuries.
It accounts for 42% of all severe injuries.
It accounts for 39% of all severe injuries.
It accounts for 25% of all severe injuries.
It accounts for 50% of all severe injuries.
correctOption: It accounts for 25% of all severe injuries.
optionExplanations: 10% does not correspond to thoracic trauma incidence; thoracic injury is significantly more prevalent in severe trauma cases.
42% represents the percentage of trauma deaths resulting from brain injury, not thoracic injury incidence.
39% represents the total trauma deaths caused by major hemorrhage (usually from torso injury), not the incidence of thoracic injury itself.
According to the reference, thoracic injury accounts for exactly 25% of all severe injuries and contributes to death in another 25%.
50% is the combined total where thoracic injury is either the primary cause or a significant contributor to death, but the baseline incidence in severe injuries is 25%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 351 (Book Page): Thoracic injury accounts for 25% of all severe injuries. In a further 25%, it may be a signifcant contributor to the subsequent death of the patient.

category: Identify the clinical features of cervical and thoracolumbar spine trauma
statement: Following a high-velocity cervical spine injury, a patient presents with a systolic blood pressure of 85 mmHg, a heart rate of 55 bpm, and warm, well-perfused extremities. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of this clinical state?
options: Unopposed vagal tone resulting from cord injury at or above T5.
Massive release of catecholamines following acute neural compression.
Hypovolaemia resulting from traumatic retroperitoneal haemorrhage.
Temporary physiological disorganisation of cord function with hyporeflexia.
Peripheral vasoconstriction causing paradoxical warm shock.
correctOption: Unopposed vagal tone resulting from cord injury at or above T5.
optionExplanations: Neurogenic shock occurs because cervical or upper thoracic cord injury disrupts the sympathetic chains, leaving the parasympathetic (vagal) tone unopposed, resulting in bradycardia and loss of peripheral vascular tone (vasodilation).
Catecholamine release would cause hypertension and tachycardia, which are transient and seen in the immediate 'sympathetic storm' rather than established neurogenic shock.
Hypovolaemic shock typically presents with tachycardia and cool, clammy peripheries, the opposite of the findings in this case.
The description of temporary disorganisation with hyporeflexia refers to spinal shock, which is a neurological state of areflexia rather than a haemodynamic state.
Neurogenic shock is characterized by vasodilation (loss of tone), not vasoconstriction; warm peripheries occur because blood is pooled in dilated peripheral vessels, not restricted from them.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Neurogenic shock . This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outflow (T5).

category: Explain management options for pathological fractures
coreConcept: Reconstructive rationale for articular pathological fractures
statement: A patient presents with a pathological fracture that extends significantly into the articular surface. What is the pathophysiological rationale for performing an en bloc excision and joint replacement rather than internal fixation?
options: Internal fixation increases the risk of systemic fat embolism syndrome in metastatic bone.
Fixation devices are unable to achieve any purchase in epiphyseal trabecular bone.
Joint replacement provides immediate access for high-dose local antibiotic delivery.
Pathological articular fractures are prone to non-union and subsequent rapid joint destruction.
En bloc excision is required to prevent the development of a secondary bursitis.
correctOption: Pathological articular fractures are prone to non-union and subsequent rapid joint destruction.
optionExplanations: While fat embolism is a concern in intramedullary procedures, it is not the primary anatomical reason for choosing arthroplasty over fixation in periarticular disease.
Fixation is possible in trabecular bone using locking technology, but in pathological states, the bone tissue itself is unreliable, making excision a more predictable functional outcome.
Local antibiotic delivery is a secondary concern usually reserved for infection, not the primary driver for choosing arthroplasty in pathological fractures.

Pathological bone around joints is structurally compromised and often biologically unable to support the rigid fixation necessary for articular surfaces, leading to early mechanical failure and debilitating degenerative changes.
Bursitis is a minor soft-tissue inflammation and does not dictate the major reconstructive choice of en bloc excision for bone failure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 422 (Book Page): If involving the joint surface or close to the joint surface, the afected area may be excised en bloc and a joint replacement performed.

category: Discuss pediatric fractures and their management
coreConcept: Salter-Harris Classification of Growth Plate Injuries
statement: Which specific injury pattern according to the Salter-Harris classification describes a fracture line that traverses simultaneously through the epiphysis, the physis, and the metaphysis?
options: Salter-Harris Type V
Salter-Harris Type IV
Salter-Harris Type I
Salter-Harris Type II
Salter-Harris Type III
correctOption: Salter-Harris Type IV
optionExplanations: Salter-Harris Type V is a compression or crush injury to the physis that often results in premature growth plate closure and is difficult to diagnose initially on radiographs.
Salter-Harris Type IV is a vertical fracture that crosses the epiphysis, the growth plate (physis), and the metaphysis, posing a high risk for osseous bridge formation and growth arrest.
Salter-Harris Type I is a simple fracture line passing only through the physis, separating the epiphysis from the metaphysis without involving the bone itself.
Salter-Harris Type II involves a fracture through the physis that exits through the metaphysis, resulting in a triangular metaphyseal bone fragment.
Salter-Harris Type III involves a fracture through the physis that exits through the epiphysis, making it an intra-articular injury requiring anatomic reduction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 402 (Book Page): [Type IV – fracture line across the epiphysis, across the physis and across the metaphysis. This injury can cause focal fusion of the physis, leading to abnormal growth.]

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
statement: Which of the following anatomical regions is most frequently associated with the development of osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in the elderly population?
options: Cervical spine (C3–C7)
Thoracic spine (T1–T10)
Distal radius
Proximal humerus
Lumbar spine (L3–S1)
correctOption: Thoracic spine (T1–T10)
optionExplanations: While the subaxial cervical spine is a common site for subluxation and burst fractures in high-energy trauma, it is not the primary site for osteoporotic wedge compression fractures.

The thoracic spine, specifically the T1 to T10 segment, is identified as the most common anatomical site for osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults due to its transitional fixed nature and susceptibility to axial load failure.

Distal radius fractures (Colles) are highly prevalent in osteoporotic patients, but they are extra-articular metaphyseal fractures, not the 'wedge compression' type characteristic of vertebral bodies.
The proximal humerus is a common site for osteoporotic periarticular fractures, but it is categorized under upper limb injuries rather than the primary site for wedge compression.

The lower lumbar spine is a frequent site for burst fractures and spondylolisthesis, but the thoracic spine remains the more common location for the specific 'wedge' compression pattern associated with osteoporosis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group [Thoracic spine (T1–T10)].

category: Educate patients and attendants regarding basic care, need for follow-up, and complications
statement: A patient with a complete T4 spinal cord injury is being managed by home health attendants. The physician must educate the family to recognize Autonomic Dysreflexia. Which clinical triad should trigger an emergency call to the surgical team?
options: Fever, localized bone tenderness, and purulent discharge.
Hypotension, tachycardia, and cold clammy peripheries.
Paralysis, decreased muscle tone, and absent bulbocavernosus reflex.
Segmental pain, progressive weakness, and expanding spinal cavities.
Hypertension, bradycardia, and a severe headache.
correctOption: Hypertension, bradycardia, and a severe headache.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. These are the classic signs of acute osteomyelitis or superficial wound infection, not an autonomic nervous system crisis.
Incorrect. This describes hypovolemic shock, which is a circulation issue rather than a paroxysmal autonomic response seen in chronic SCI.
Incorrect. These are the characteristics of 'spinal shock,' which is a temporary physiological loss of function immediately following injury, not the late-complication autonomic dysreflexia.
Incorrect. This constellation describes post-traumatic syringomyelia, a chronic complication involving the formation of a syrinx, rather than an acute paroxysmal syndrome.

Correct. Autonomic dysreflexia is a medical emergency in SCI patients (above T6) where a noxious stimulus (like a full bladder) causes massive sympathetic discharge leading to life-threatening hypertension and compensatory bradycardia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 383 (Book Page): Autonomic dysreflexia ... is a paroxysmal syndrome of hypertension, hyperhidrosis (above the level of injury), bradycardia, flushing and headache in response to noxious visceral and other stimuli.

category: Discuss treatment options for scoliosis
statement: What is the standard radiographic measurement used by clinicians to quantify the severity of a lateral spinal curvature in scoliosis?
options: The Morin Index
The Cobb Angle
The Herring Classification
The Hilgenreiner Line
The Southwick Angle
correctOption: The Cobb Angle
optionExplanations: The Morin index is an ultrasound measurement indicating the percentage of the femoral head covered by the acetabulum.
The Cobb angle is the universal standard for measuring the degrees of curvature in scoliosis on a posteroanterior radiograph.
The Herring classification relates to the height of the lateral pillar in Perthes' disease.
Hilgenreiner’s line is a horizontal line through the triradiate cartilage used in diagnosing hip dysplasia (DDH).
The Southwick angle is specifically used to measure the severity of a slip in capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 608 (Book Page): The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defines severity and guides treatment.

category: Describe principles of fracture healing
coreConcept: Perren's Strain Theory in Bone Differentiation
statement: According to Perren’s theory of fracture healing, which maximum strain level is necessary to allow for the differentiation into hard callus and progressive mineralization?
options: Strain exceeding 100%
Strain under 50%
Strain under 100%
Strain less than 2%
Strain under 10%
correctOption: Strain less than 2%
optionExplanations: Strains exceeding 100% prevent the stabilization of even mesenchymal tissue, typically leading to failure of the healing process.
Strain of 50% is not a specific threshold cited in Perren's theory; it falls within the range for fibrous tissue formation.
Strain under 100% allows for the formation of fibrous tissue but is too high to permit stable mineralization.
Mineralization and hard callus formation strictly require a very stable environment where the mechanical strain is reduced to less than 2%.
Strain under 10% leads to the development of soft callus but is still insufficient for the formation of hard callus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 425 (Book Page): The amount of strain determines the nature of tissue it differentiates into: under 100% leads to fbrous tissue, under 10% soft callus, less than 2% hard callus and progressive mineralisation (Perren’s theory of bone healing).

category: Explain biomechanics of gait and malalignment injuries
statement: In the analysis of human locomotion, what is the standard percentage distribution of the normal gait cycle between the stance and swing phases?
options: 80% stance phase and 20% swing phase
70% stance phase and 30% swing phase
60% stance phase and 40% swing phase
50% stance phase and 50% swing phase
40% stance phase and 60% swing phase
correctOption: 60% stance phase and 40% swing phase
optionExplanations: Incorrect. 80/20 would represent a significant alteration in gait speed or pathology, not normal locomotion.
Incorrect. 70/30 is not the standard physiological distribution for a normal adult gait.
Correct. In a normal gait cycle, the stance phase (initial contact to toe-off) occupies 60% of the cycle, while the swing phase (toe-off to the next contact) occupies 40%.
Incorrect. The gait cycle is not evenly split; weight-bearing (stance) requires more time for stability.
Incorrect. The swing phase is the shorter portion of the gait cycle, representing 40%, not 60%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 473 (Book Page): There are two main stages: the stance phase (60%) and the swing phase (40%).

category: Classify abdominal trauma based on mechanism and organ involvement
statement: When assessing individual organ injury in the abdomen, why is it recommended that the portal vein be shunted or repaired rather than ligated in a physiologically compromised patient?
options: Ligation causes immediate hepatic necrosis in 100% of cases.
Ligation causes immediate and irreversible renal failure.
Ligation of the portal vein carries a mortality rate exceeding 50%.
The portal vein is the sole blood supply to the gallbladder.
The portal vein provides only 10% of the liver's oxygen requirements.
correctOption: Ligation of the portal vein carries a mortality rate exceeding 50%.
optionExplanations: While it causes severe congestion and ischemia, it is not 100% immediate necrosis, but the systemic consequences are often lethal.
The primary effect is on the splanchnic circulation and the liver, not primarily renal failure (though it can occur as a secondary event).
Ligating the portal vein leads to massive intestinal congestion and hepatic failure, with a high mortality rate (>50%), necessitating repair or shunting.
The cystic artery supplies the gallbladder, not the portal vein.
The portal vein provides about 70-80% of the liver's blood flow and significant oxygenation, making it vital.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): Damage to the portal vein must be repaired, as tying of the portal vein carries a greater than 50% mortality rate. If it is not technically feasible to repair the vein at the time of surgery, it should be shunted and the patient referred to a specialist centre.

category: Outline the early surgical and supportive management plan to prevent morbidity and mortality
statement: A trauma team is assessing a multiply injured patient's suitability for Early Total Care (ETC) versus Damage Control Surgery (DCS). According to established resuscitation markers, which physiological parameter suggests the patient is under-resuscitated and requires DCS?
options: Venous lactate <2 mmol/L
Core body temperature of 36.5°C
Venous lactate >5 mmol/L
Pulse rate of 90 beats per minute
Urine output >30 mL/h
correctOption: Venous lactate >5 mmol/L
optionExplanations: Lactate <2 mmol/L indicates the patient is well-resuscitated and likely a candidate for Early Total Care (ETC).
36.5°C is a normal temperature. Hypothermia (<35°C) is what triggers a move towards Damage Control Surgery.
A lactate level above 5 mmol/L indicates severe occult tissue hypoxia and metabolic acidosis, meaning the patient cannot tolerate long, definitive operations.
A pulse of 90 is within the normal range for a resuscitated patient; tachycardia (>100) would be a more concerning sign for instability.
Urine output >30 mL/h is a sign of adequate organ perfusion, favoring ETC rather than DCS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 359 (Book Page): Summary box 27.6 Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation... ● >5 mmol/L – DCS

category: Outline principles of management
coreConcept: Venous Lactate as a Resuscitation Marker
statement: A 28-year-old polytrauma patient is undergoing resuscitation. The trauma lead is assessing the suitability for Early Total Care (ETC) versus Damage Control Surgery (DCS). Which venous lactate profile suggests that the patient is currently under-resuscitated and may require DCS if surgery is urgent?
options: Venous lactate of 1.5 mmol/L with a stable trend
Venous lactate > 5.0 mmol/L, indicating immediate DCS
Venous lactate < 1.0 mmol/L
Venous lactate of 2.5 mmol/L with a downward trend
Venous lactate of 3.5 mmol/L
correctOption: Venous lactate of 3.5 mmol/L
optionExplanations: A level of 1.5 mmol/L is normal, indicating the patient has likely restored aerobic metabolism and is fit for definitive reconstruction.

While a lactate > 5 mmol/L is a clear indication for DCS, the question specifically asks for the level indicating 'under-resuscitation' where DCS or 'further resuscitation' are both options; >5 is the definitive cutoff for absolute DCS.
A lactate level less than 2 mmol/L generally suggests adequate resuscitation, making the patient suitable for ETC rather than DCS.
When lactate is in the 2–3 mmol/L range, the trend is critical; a downward trend suggests successful resuscitation and potential suitability for ETC.
A lactate level > 3 mmol/L is the specific threshold defining under-resuscitation, necessitating further resuscitation or the adoption of a DCS approach if intervention is time-sensitive.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): An elevated lactate (>3 mmol/L) suggests the patient is under-resuscitated and should either have a period of further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent.

category: Outline management principles
statement: Management of a patient with suspected pelvic fracture requires specific precautions during the primary and secondary surveys. Which of the following is an established clinical management principle?
options: Rely on the absence of a pelvic hematoma to rule out internal pelvic bleeding
Check for pelvic stability by applying lateral-to-medial pressure to the iliac crests
Perform a formal log-roll early in the primary survey to check the back
Remove the pelvic binder as soon as the patient is placed on the CT gantry
Utilize a 'scoop stretcher' to minimize the need to roll the patient more than 20°
correctOption: Utilize a 'scoop stretcher' to minimize the need to roll the patient more than 20°
optionExplanations: Pelvic bleeding is often retroperitoneal and can accommodate up to 3 liters of blood without any external hematoma or skin bruising being visible.
This is 'springing' the pelvis. It is an abandoned technique because it is clinically unreliable and dangerous for the patient's hemodynamic stability.
Formal log-rolling is deferred because it provides minimal information during the primary survey and carries a significant risk of disrupting pelvic clots.
A pelvic binder must never be removed until a fracture is radiographically excluded. Removing it on the CT gantry could lead to sudden hemodynamic collapse.
Scoop stretchers allow the patient to be moved with minimal disturbance to the pelvic ring, keeping any necessary roll to less than 20 degrees, which is the standard safety margin.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 357 (Book Page): Modern ‘scoop stretchers’ mean that there is no requirement to roll any patient more than 20° until a pelvic fracture has been excluded. Formal log-rolling of the blunt trauma patient to examine the back during the primary survey adds minimal useful clinical information... and may cause harm to a patient with a pelvic fracture.

category: Discuss risk factors for osteoporosis
statement: A patient with a chronic T4 spinal cord injury is diagnosed with progressive bone density loss in the lower extremities. What is the fundamental pathological cause of this bone loss in this specific clinical context?
options: Mechanical unloading of the skeleton leading to disuse osteoporosis
Secondary hypercalcemia resulting from renal impairment
Direct traumatic injury to the medullary nutrient arteries
Hormonal shifts triggered by damage to the pituitary axis
Inflammatory cytokine release during autonomic dysreflexia
correctOption: Mechanical unloading of the skeleton leading to disuse osteoporosis
optionExplanations: Disuse osteoporosis occurs because bone deposition depends on mechanical stress (Wolff’s Law); spinal cord injury results in prolonged unloading, making bone density loss inevitable.
Renal impairment can affect mineral balance, but the text attributes the bone loss in spinal cord injury directly to disuse.
Traumatic injury to nutrient arteries causes acute osteonecrosis or delayed union, but the generalized density loss following paralysis is a systemic disuse phenomenon.
While the pituitary can be affected in TBI, spinal cord injury induces osteoporosis primarily through the lack of weight-bearing and mechanical tension.
Autonomic dysreflexia is a paroxysmal sympathetic syndrome but is not the primary driver of the biochemical cascade of bone resorption in this group.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 404 (Book Page): Disuse osteoporosis is an inevitable consequence of spinal cord injury and fragility fractures may occur.

category: Outline the management plan
statement: A 25-year-old male presents with pain in his right wrist after falling on an outstretched hand. Initial radiographs are negative for a fracture, but there is marked tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. What is the appropriate management plan?
options: Reassure the patient and allow immediate return to heavy lifting
Immobilize in a below-elbow cast and repeat radiographs in 10–14 days
Apply an elasticated bandage and review in the outpatient clinic in 6 weeks
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation with a compression screw
Perform a technetium-99 bone scan within the first 24 hours to confirm the diagnosis
correctOption: Immobilize in a below-elbow cast and repeat radiographs in 10–14 days
optionExplanations: Dismissing the patient risks missing a scaphoid fracture, which has a high rate of non-union and avascular necrosis due to retrograde blood supply.
Correct. The protocol for clinical suspicion of a scaphoid fracture with negative X-rays is immobilization followed by repeat clinical and radiographic assessment in 10-14 days.
A bandage provides insufficient immobilization for a scaphoid fracture; a cast is required.
Surgery is reserved for displaced or confirmed unstable fractures, not for those with negative initial imaging.
While a bone scan can be used, the 'standard protocol' described is repeated examination and radiography at 10-14 days.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): If a fracture is not evident on the initial radiographs and the patient remains tender in the anatomical snuf box, then treat as a suspected scaphoid fracture until a fracture is actively excluded. The standard protocol... is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later.

category: Apply the principles of primary survey (ABCDE) for rapid assessment and stabilization
statement: In the physiological assessment of tissue perfusion during the primary survey and resuscitation, how should a venous lactate level of 4 mmol/L be interpreted by the trauma team?
options: The patient is in a normal state, as lactate only becomes significant when >10 mmol/L.
The patient should be immediately cleared for definitive spinal fixation within 36 hours.
The patient is adequately resuscitated and suitable for early total care (ETC).
This is a sign of respiratory alkalosis requiring immediate hyperventilation.
The patient is under-resuscitated and may require damage control surgery (DCS).
correctOption: The patient is under-resuscitated and may require damage control surgery (DCS).
optionExplanations: Lactate becomes clinically significant in trauma decision-making once it exceeds the normal threshold of 2 mmol/L.
Definitive fixation (ETC) requires a resuscitated state (Lactate <2), not an elevated level of 4.
Normal lactate is <2 mmol/L; a value of 4 is significantly elevated and indicates inadequate tissue perfusion.
Lactic acidosis is a form of metabolic acidosis, not respiratory alkalosis.
Lactate >3 is a red flag for occult shock or under-resuscitation. If the level was >5, DCS would be even more strongly indicated.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): An elevated lactate (>3 mmol/L) suggests the patient is under-resuscitated and should either have a period of further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent.

category: Outline management principles
statement: Early total care (ETC) is a management strategy for musculoskeletal injuries in a polytrauma patient. Within what time frame must defnitive fxation of all unstable long bone and pelvic fractures be achieved to qualify as ETC?
options: Within 36 hours of the injury
Within 48 hours of the injury
Within 72 hours of the injury
Within 12 hours of the injury
Within 24 hours of the injury
correctOption: Within 36 hours of the injury
optionExplanations: ETC is defned as the defnitive management of a patient's injuries within 36 hours after initial resuscitation, facilitating early mobilisation and reduced ICU stay.
Forty-eight hours exceeds the standard defnition for ETC as per the reference text.
Seventy-two hours is the window for commencing enteral nutrition but is twice as long as the window for ETC defnitive fxation.
Twelve hours is typically the window for initial debridement of open fractures but is shorter than the defned window for ETC.
While 24 hours is a common goal for stabilization, it does not match the specifc 36-hour defnition for ETC provided in the reference.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): For musculoskeletal injuries, ETC allows defnitive fxation of all unstable long bone, spinal and pelvic fractures within 36 hours of injury.

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
coreConcept: Concurrent geriatric sites of osteoporotic injury following falls.
statement: An 82-year-old patient presents after a low-energy fall from a standing height. Based on the common sites of fragility fractures, which anatomical combination of injuries should be immediately prioritized for evaluation?
options: Radial head dislocation and ulnar shaft greenstick fracture
Talar neck fracture and calcaneal avulsion
Cervical spine subluxation and sternal fracture
Proximal femoral (hip) fracture and multiple rib fractures
Isolated scapular fracture and distal ulnar styloid avulsion
correctOption: Proximal femoral (hip) fracture and multiple rib fractures
optionExplanations: Greenstick fractures are exclusive to the plastic bone of the skeletally immature (pediatric), not the brittle bone of the osteoporotic elderly.
Talar neck and calcaneal fractures are generally associated with significant vertical energy (falls from heights), not standing falls.
Sternal fractures combined with spine disruption are markers of high-energy decelerations, not the typical osteoporotic fragility pattern.
The text explicitly notes that older adults falling even a few steps (low energy) commonly sustain fractures of the hip and ribs, making these prioritized sites.
Scapular fractures are rare in low-energy geriatric falls, usually requiring high-energy trauma as seen in high-speed collisions.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 354 (Book Page): An older adult patient falling down a few steps can easily sustain a hip fracture, multiple rib fractures and a small subdural haemorrhage.

category: Differentiate between complete and incomplete fractures
statement: In the context of fracture mechanics, how does 'strain' influence the physiological loop of indirect bone healing in a healing incomplete fracture?
options: Absolute stability (0% strain) is required for callus formation
High strain (>100%) promotes direct lamellar bone formation
Strain under 10% promotes the formation of soft callus
Strain has no effect on the differentiation of fracture hematoma
High strain leads immediately to hard callus mineralisation
correctOption: Strain under 10% promotes the formation of soft callus
optionExplanations: Absolute stability (0% strain) leads to primary/direct bone healing, which skips the callus formation phase.
High strain (>100%) leads to fibrous tissue rather than bone, which can cause non-union.
Correct. According to the text (Perren's theory), strain under 10% is necessary for the differentiation into soft callus.
Strain is the primary mechanical stimulus that determines whether the hematoma becomes fibrous tissue or bone.
Hard callus mineralization requires even lower strain (<2%) following the soft callus phase; high strain prevents it.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): The amount of strain determines the nature of tissue it differentiates into... under 10% soft callus, less than 2% hard callus

category: Define severe trauma and recognize its impact on morbidity and mortality
coreConcept: Clinical Triggers for Tranexamic Acid Administration
statement: Tranexamic acid is standard in severe trauma protocols to reduce mortality. Which specific criterion mandates its administration to suspected bleeding patients within the first hour of injury to ensure maximum efficacy?
options: Systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or pulse >110 bpm
Bilateral long bone fractures with gross deformity
A venous lactate level exceeding 4.0 mmol/L
A Glasgow Coma Scale score of less than 8
Presence of a visible 'sucking chest wound'
correctOption: Systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or pulse >110 bpm
optionExplanations: A heart rate over 110 or systolic BP under 110 are the standardized triggers for TXA, as it significantly reduces mortality when given early.
Long bone fractures suggest trauma, but the systemic trigger for TXA is hemodynamic instability indicative of major hemorrhage.
While lactate is a marker of shock, the standardized clinical protocol for TXA is based on heart rate and blood pressure.
GCS is used to assess head injury severity, not as a primary trigger for antifibrinolytic therapy.
An open pneumothorax requires immediate occlusive dressing and drainage, but TXA is indicated based on hemodynamic parameters of bleeding.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage, including those with a systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or a pulse of over 110 per minute.

category: Discuss the role of bedside and imaging investigations in diagnosis
coreConcept: The Rule of 2s in Orthopedic Imaging
statement: In clinical practice, what is the 'Rule of 2s' protocol recommended for a patient with suspected scaphoid injury whose initial radiographs are interpreted as normal?
options: Apply two different types of splints for two months
Order two nuclear medicine scans separated by two days
Perform a bilateral aspiration of both wrists to compare fluid
Repeat the radiographs after 10–14 days if symptoms persist
Obtain two MRI sequences and two CT slices within 2 hours
correctOption: Repeat the radiographs after 10–14 days if symptoms persist
optionExplanations: The 'Rule of 2s' refers to imaging (2 views, 2 joints, 2 occasions, 2 sides), not the type or duration of bracing.
Nuclear medicine is an alternative if available, but the standard protocol emphasizes serial radiography over 2 occasions.
Aspiration is used for infection or crystal arthropathy, not for diagnosing occult scaphoid fractures.
Scaphoid fractures are notoriously occult initially. Waiting 10-14 days allows for bone resorption at the fracture line, making it visible on follow-up plain films.
The protocol focuses on the timing of serial plain films, not multiple advanced imaging sequences within 2 hours.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): 2 occasions – sometimes the fracture may not be initially visible; a second series of radiographs should be undertaken after 10–14 days if suspicion of bony injury persists. The classic injury here is a scaphoid fracture.

category: Discuss the principles of management
coreConcept: Physiological Indicators for Early Total Care
statement: When deciding between 'Early Total Care' (ETC) and 'Damage Control Surgery' (DCS) for the management of orthopaedic injuries, which clinical marker is considered a reliable physiological index of adequate tissue perfusion to support definitive reconstruction within 36 hours?
options: The presence of a bounding pedal pulse
A urinary output of at least 15 mL/h
A core body temperature maintained above 37.5°C
A serum bicarbonate level of exactly 24 mmol/L
A venous lactate level of less than 2 mmol/L
correctOption: A venous lactate level of less than 2 mmol/L
optionExplanations: Pedal pulses only assess macrovascular flow to the extremity and do not reflect systemic tissue perfusion, core oxygenation, or the presence of occult metabolic acidosis which determines surgical readiness.
Target urine output for a trauma patient to indicate adequate organ perfusion is typically >30 mL/h, not 15 mL/h. 15 mL/h would suggest inadequate renal perfusion and potential under-resuscitation.

A temperature >37.5°C may actually suggest an inflammatory response or pyrexia; the requirement for ETC is that the patient should not be hypothermic (<35°C). Normal core temperature (36-37°C) is required, but being hyperthermic is not a requisite index for ETC.

While bicarbonate reflects acid-base balance, it is a calculated value on many blood gas machines and is influenced by respiratory compensation, whereas lactate is a direct product of anaerobic metabolism and a better marker of tissue-level hypoxia.

Venous lactate is a critical surrogate for tissue perfusion. Levels <2 mmol/L suggest successful aerobic respiration and adequate oxygen delivery, allowing the body to tolerate the further 'second hit' of definitive surgery (ETC). Levels above 3-5 mmol/L indicate significant anaerobic metabolism and a need for DCS.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): Lactate levels are also a good indicator of tissue perfusion and should rapidly return to normal. In this situation, it is usually safe for the surgeon to proceed with defnitive repair or reconstruction of injured organs. ... A normal lactate (<2 mmol/L) is a sign that the patient is probably resuscitated and suitable for ETC. An elevated lactate (>3 mmol/L) suggests the patient is under-resuscitated and should either have a period of further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment using ATLS framework with emphasis on Glasgow Coma Scale
statement: During the Primary Survey of a trauma patient with a suspected traumatic brain injury (TBI), what is the target systolic blood pressure recommended by the ATLS framework to maintain cerebral perfusion?
options: >140 mmHg
>90 mmHg
70–80 mmHg
Any pressure that produces a palpable carotid pulse
correctOption: >90 mmHg
optionExplanations: Targeting >140 mmHg could exacerbate intracranial hemorrhage or cause excessive bleeding from other sites without proven benefit in the initial survey.
While 110-120 mmHg is normal, the specific minimum threshold for 'safe' permissive hypotension in TBI according to the text is 90 mmHg.
In head injury, cerebral autoregulation is often impaired. A systolic BP >90 mmHg is required to maintain adequate Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) and prevent secondary brain injury.
70-80 mmHg is appropriate for permissive hypotension in isolated torso trauma to minimize bleeding, but is too low for a patient with TBI.
A carotid pulse only confirms a systolic pressure around 60-70 mmHg, which is insufficient for a head-injured patient.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 355 (Book Page): For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.

category: Describe multidisciplinary approach in managing scoliosis
statement: A 14-year-old female is diagnosed with Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS). According to standard clinical classification, which age range correctly defines this category of scoliosis?
options: Birth to 3 years
Greater than 18 years
3 years to 10 years
Less than 10 years
11 to 18 years
correctOption: 11 to 18 years
optionExplanations: Scoliosis appearing from birth to 3 years is classified as infantile scoliosis, which has a distinct natural history and management protocol.
Onset at maturity (greater than 18 years) is classified as adult scoliosis, which often involves degenerative changes not seen in the adolescent form.
The range of 3 to 10 years is generally categorized under juvenile idiopathic scoliosis or included in the broader 'early onset' category.
Early-onset scoliosis is specifically defined as a curve appearing before the age of 10 years, carrying higher risks for pulmonary issues.
Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis (AIS) is the most common form, appearing between ages 11 and 18, typically coinciding with the pubertal growth spurt.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 608 (Book Page): Table 44.12 Classification of idiopathic scoliosis. Type: Adolescent. Age at onset: 11–18 years.

category: Identify appropriate diagnostic investigations, especially imaging
coreConcept: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip Screening Timing
statement: According to neonatal screening guidelines for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), at what postnatal age should sonographic screening be performed for infants identified as 'at-risk'?
options: Between 4 and 6 weeks of age
Within the first 48 hours of birth
At 12 weeks to ensure physiological laxity has resolved
Only after 4 months once the ossific nucleus appears
Between the first and second weeks of life
correctOption: Between 4 and 6 weeks of age
optionExplanations: The 4-to-6 week window is ideal as it allows early maternal hormonal effects to dissipate while still allowing treatment to begin by 6 weeks.
Physiological laxity is common at birth due to maternal hormones, leading to false positives if scanned too early.
12 weeks is too late to start primary treatment for many severe cases of dysplasia, as acetabular remodeling potential is maximal earlier.
Radiography is used after 4 months; waiting this long for a scan would delay critical early intervention with harnesses.
Many hips stabilize spontaneously within the first few weeks; scanning before 4 weeks often leads to over-treatment of postural instability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 616 (Book Page): Screening scans should be performed between 4 and 6 weeks of age and treatment, when necessary, started by 6 weeks.

category: Describe principles of fracture healing
statement: A 40-year-old male smoker with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a tibial fracture that shows no clinical or radiological improvement 16 weeks post-injury. Which type of non-union is most likely considering the biological compromise of the host?
options: Hypertrophic non-union
Atrophic non-union
Delayed union
Pseudarthrosis
Infected non-union
correctOption: Atrophic non-union
optionExplanations: Hypertrophic non-union is characterized by excessive movement at the fracture site with a healthy biological response, unlike the biological failure seen in smokers and diabetics.
Atrophic non-union is caused by poor biology, often related to diminished blood supply, smoking, and systemic diseases like diabetes that impair the healing response.
Delayed union is a fracture that is merely slow to heal, but the term non-union is applied when there is no potential to heal without intervention, often assessed after several months.
Pseudarthrosis is the endpoint of a non-union where a 'false joint' forms, but it does not specifically describe the biological cause (atrophy).
While infection can cause non-union, atrophic non-union is the specific term for failures primarily driven by the metabolic and vascular compromise described.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): In an atrophic non-union, the problem is generally a biological one, with a lack of stimulus or blood supply. ... Well-known factors that slow down bone healing include diabetes mellitus (doubles time to union), diminished blood supply ... smoking.

category: Identify common sites of osteoporotic fractures
statement: Regarding injuries to the thoracic spine (T1–T10), which specific type of fracture is identified as the most common within this anatomical group in older adults?
options: Chance flexion-distraction injuries
Transverse process avulsion fractures
Comminuted burst fractures with retropulsion
Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures
Rotational type C fracture-dislocations
correctOption: Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures
optionExplanations: Chance fractures are specifically flexion-distraction injuries often associated with lap-belt use and are typically seen at the thoracolumbar junction rather than being characteristic of osteoporosis in the T1-T10 range.

Transverse process avulsion fractures are typically the result of direct trauma or extreme paraspinal muscle contraction and are not identified as the characteristic osteoporotic injury in the thoracic region.

While burst fractures involve the vertebral body, they are characterized by comminution and interpedicular widening, whereas the simple wedge compression is the definitive osteoporotic presentation cited for this group.

Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures occur when the cancellous bone of the vertebral body collapses under normal or low-energy loads due to decreased bone mineral density, making them the most frequent thoracic injury in the elderly.
Type C injuries involve high-energy rotation often accompanied by rib dislocations and significant internal injuries, which contrasts with the low-energy mechanism typical of osteoporotic fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): Osteoporotic wedge compression fractures in older adults are the commonest injury in this group.

category: Interpret characteristic radiological features of OI used for diagnosis and monitoring
coreConcept: Stabilization priorities in Osteogenesis Imperfecta bone.
statement: When interpreting radiographs to plan the stabilization of long bone fractures or osteotomies in a patient with Osteogenesis Imperfecta, which surgical stabilization method is radiologically and clinically preferred over plate fixation?
options: Intramedullary techniques
Circumferential cerclage wiring
Monolateral external fixation
Multiple Kirschner wire transfixion
Rigid tension band wiring
correctOption: Intramedullary techniques
optionExplanations: Intramedullary devices are preferred because they provide internal support across the entire bone length, reducing the risk of 'stress risers' that plates might create in brittle bone.
Cerclage wiring alone is insufficient to stabilize axial loads and can compromise periosteal blood supply, which is counterproductive in OI management.
External fixation poses a risk of pin-site fractures and stress risers in brittle OI bone, making it less favorable than internal options.
K-wires are often too flexible for long bone stabilization in OI and lack the load-sharing capacity needed for brittle cortices.
Tension band wiring is specific to certain periarticular fractures (e.g., olecranon) and does not provide the axial support needed for the long bones typically monitored in OI.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 594 (Book Page): Intramedullary techniques for stabilisation of fractures or osteotomies are preferred to plate fxation.

category: List the indications for urgent surgical referral and definitive management
statement: A patient with a head injury requires an urgent referral for CT imaging. Which criteria mandate this scan be performed within 1 hour of presentation?
options: Use of anticoagulant medications such as warfarin or rivaroxaban
The patient is older than 65 years of age
A dangerous mechanism of injury such as a fall from a height
Retrograde amnesia of events occurring more than 30 minutes before injury
Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of less than 13 at any point
correctOption: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of less than 13 at any point
optionExplanations: Coagulopathy is a risk factor requiring a scan, but the 1-hour 'urgent' window is reserved for signs of immediate clinical deterioration like low GCS.
Age >65 is an indication for CT, but it is typically categorized under the 8-hour window unless other acute deficits are present.
A dangerous mechanism is an indication for a scan within 8 hours, provided the patient's GCS remains high.
Isolated retrograde amnesia >30 minutes is an indication for a scan within the 8-hour window according to NICE guidelines.
A GCS <13 indicates potential intracranial catastrophe or significant brain injury requiring immediate (within 1 hour) neurosurgical evaluation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 341 (Book Page): Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point

category: Describe radiological features of osteomyelitis
statement: Which radiological finding on a plain radiograph typically appears first, occurring between 5 and 7 days after the onset of acute osteomyelitis symptoms?
options: A central lucent cyst with a sclerotic wall
Pathological fracture through a sequestrum
Complete dissolution of the medullary canal
Osteopenia and subtle periosteal new bone
A thick involucrum around the diaphysis
correctOption: Osteopenia and subtle periosteal new bone
optionExplanations: This describes a Brodie’s abscess, which is a chronic, localized form of infection, not a finding at the 5-7 day mark of an acute infection.
Pathological fractures occur in bone weakened by chronic infection or tumors; they do not appear within the first week of acute infection.
Complete medullary dissolution is an extreme feature of uncontrolled chronic infection, not a typical early finding.
While radiographs are normal initially, by the end of the first week, inflammatory hyperaemia leads to localized osteopenia and the lifted periosteum begins to lay down new bone.
An involucrum takes weeks to form as it is the body's chronic attempt to stabilize a bone containing a sequestrum.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 604 (Book Page): After 5–7 days, plain radiographs may show subtle abnormality with osteopenia and periosteal new bone formation.

category: Outline plan for definitive management and multidisciplinary care
coreConcept: Rationale for DAIR in Prosthetic Joint Infection
statement: In the multidisciplinary care of a suspected prosthetic joint infection (PJI), what is the primary mechanical requirement for implementing the 'Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention' (DAIR) management strategy?
options: Postponing surgical intervention until the bioflm has matured to allow systemic antibiotics to penetrate the matrix
A well-fixed prosthesis to allow for radical soft tissue excision and exchange of modular parts
Retention of the original modular components to prevent disruption of the established joint kinetics
The presence of a loose implant to allow antibiotic irrigation of the cement-bone interface
Exclusive use of arthroscopic debridement to maintain the integrity of the joint capsule
correctOption: A well-fixed prosthesis to allow for radical soft tissue excision and exchange of modular parts
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Bioflm maturation makes bacteria more resistant to both the host immune system and antibiotics (page 596). Surgical intervention should be prompt to disrupt the bioflm community before it becomes impenetrable.

Correct. DAIR requires the prosthesis to be well-fixed. The mechanical stability of the implant allows the surgeon to perform radical excision of all infected soft tissues and necrotic bone, while exchanging modular components to physically remove surface bioflm.
Incorrect. In a successful DAIR procedure, modular components (such as polyethylene liners or femoral heads) must be exchanged because they are common sites for bioflm accumulation (page 602).

Incorrect. A loose infected implant is an absolute contraindication for DAIR; loose implants must be removed because the bioflm residing at the bone-implant interface cannot be eradicated without extraction (page 602).

Incorrect. The text specifies that DAIR cannot be effectively achieved through arthroscopy because it requires total excision of infected soft tissue and modular exchange, which necessitates an open approach (page 602).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 581 (Book Page): Debridement, antibiotics and implant retention - ‘DAIR’. This can only be undertaken if the prosthesis is well fxed. DAIR is not a form of washout as all infected soft tissue and necrotic bone must be fully excised and modular components exchanged.

category: Identify causes of pathological fractures
statement: A patient with metabolic bone disease is prescribed cyclical bisphosphonates to reduce the incidence of pathological fractures. For which underlying cause of bone fragility is this pharmacological step most indicated in the pediatric population?
options: Congenital pseudarthrosis of the tibia
Osteomyelitis of the femoral neck
Salter-Harris Type V physeal injury
Persistent femoral neck anteversion
Osteogenesis imperfecta
correctOption: Osteogenesis imperfecta
optionExplanations: Congenital pseudarthrosis is a rare bowing/fracture condition often associated with neurofibromatosis; treatment is usually orthotic or surgical rather than cyclical bisphosphonates.
Osteomyelitis is an infectious condition requiring surgical debridement and antibiotics; bisphosphonates are not the primary treatment for infectious bone destruction.
Salter-Harris Type V is a crush injury to the growth plate that can lead to growth arrest; it is a traumatic event, not a metabolic disease requiring bisphosphonates.
Femoral neck anteversion is a rotational normal variant that usually improves with growth and does not involve the brittle bone pathology addressed by bisphosphonates.

Osteogenesis imperfecta involves a qualitative/quantitative abnormality of collagen leading to brittle bones; bisphosphonates are used here to inhibit osteoclast activity and strengthen the weakened bone.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 615 (Book Page): Cyclical bisphosphonate treatment decreases bone resorption and turnover. This reduces bone pain and the fracture rate, promoting weight-bearing mobility and bone strength [in Osteogenesis Imperfecta].

category: Identify orthopedic complications
statement: In the pathological process of chronic osteomyelitis, what term specifically describes the fragment of dead bone that has become separated from the surrounding living tissue?
options: Involucrum
Sequestrum
Physis
Callus
Osteophyte
correctOption: Sequestrum
optionExplanations: Involucrum refers to the new bone that is laid down around the infected area by the periosteum, not the dead fragments themselves.
Sequestrum is the medical term for a piece of dead bone that has become detached during the process of sequestration in chronic osteomyelitis.
The physis is the growth plate responsible for longitudinal growth in children, not a byproduct of infection.
Callus is a bridge of specialized tissue (soft or hard) that forms during the natural repair process of a fracture, not a necrotic fragment.
An osteophyte is a bony outgrowth often associated with degenerative joint disease (osteoarthritis).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 575 (Book Page): The infected bone reacts to the infection by separating dead fragments of bone (sequestration) and forming sinuses to drain pus and discharge small bone fragments.

category: Discuss the role of surgical and non-surgical interventions in improving function and quality of life
statement: The Hueter–Volkmann principle describes a fundamental physiological loop utilized in non-surgical pediatric orthopaedic interventions. How does this principle explain the success of bracing in improving deformity?
options: Tensile forces inhibit growth while compression stimulates it
Growth occurs only at the epiphysis and never at the physis
Electrical signals in the periosteum convert cartilage to cortical bone
Compressive forces inhibit growth while tensile forces stimulate it
Bone is only deposited in areas where there is no mechanical stress
correctOption: Compressive forces inhibit growth while tensile forces stimulate it
optionExplanations: This is the opposite of the Hueter-Volkmann principle. Compression slows down the growth plate's chondrocyte proliferation.
Growth primarily occurs at the physis (growth plate). The epiphysis is the ossification center.
